Photograph: Loren Elliott/Reuters View image in fullscreen Woolworths increased the prices of at least four key products during its ‘Price Freeze’ promotion, pricing data reveals. Photograph: Loren Elliott/Reuters Woolworths Woolworths increased prices of at least four ‘family staples’ during ‘Price Freeze’ promotion Exclusive: Analysis shows cost of chicken fillets, potatoes and donuts rose during supermarket giant’s three-month promotion Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Catie McLeod Consumer affairs reporter Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Woolworths raised prices for popular items – including a 33% mark up on chicken fillets – within days of promising to freeze prices on 300 “family staples” for three months to help customers with the cost of living. Pricing data, compiled by comparison website CW Scanner and provided to Guardian Australia, shows the supermarket chain increasing the prices of at least four key products after starting the three-month “Price Freeze” promotion on 1 May. The supermarket nearly doubled the price of a 420g can of Woolworths “Mexican Style 3 Bean Mix” during the promotional period – from 60c to $1 on 17 June – the data shows. Woolworths dropped the price back to 60c on 17 August. Woolworths posts $1.14bn profit in cost-of-living crisis – but CEO says it’s not thanks to rising shelf prices Read more Woolworths declined to comment on the analysis. But it is understood that it justified the increases during the “Price Freeze” because it regarded the previous prices as promotional prices, rather than the “standard shelf price” for each product. When the price freeze was announced , the Woolworths chief executive officer, Amanda Bardwell, said the supermarket wanted to help customers who were concerned about how inflation driven by the war on Iran was affecting household budgets. “That’s why, for the next three months, we’re freezing the shelf price on 300 staples that families rely on most, like eggs, chicken breast fillets, pasta, beef sausages and nappies,” Bardwell said in a press release on 30 April. “It’s our promise that the shelf price you see on these items today is the most you’ll pay for the next three months. We’ll invest to absorb any extra costs that are agreed with suppliers on these products to make that happen.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Prof Jana Bowden, a marketing expert and chair of ethics at Macquarie University’s business school, said raising prices after claiming they had been fixed was “akin to not delivering on the everyday consumer’s interpretation of a ‘price freeze’ promise”. “How is the consumer expected to know what the start prices were before the campaign or even after the campaign started?” Bowden said. “No consumer walks into a supermarket with the insights of how the prices for the hundreds of products that they buy vary over a day, week, month or year – nor should they have to.” The analysis comes at a time of high scrutiny of the pricing tactics used by Woolworths – and rival Coles – after landmark court cases involving both companies. Woolworths is awaiting the verdict in the federal court case brought against it by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), with the watchdog alleging the supermarket misled shoppers with effectively fake discounts on its “Prices Dropped” campaign. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Prices unfrozen During its price freeze period, Woolworths increased the retail price of 350g packs of RSPCA-approved chicken breast fillets by 33%. While a customer would have paid $9 for the chicken breast fillets on 29 April, the price increased to $12 on 5 May. It then alternated between $9 and $12 twice more during the “Price Freeze”. But, after the promotional period ended, the price dropped to $4.20 on 17 August. Before the promotion, Woolworths’ 2kg bags of washed potatoes had consistently followed a routine high-low pricing pattern alternating between $6 and $8. This appears to have occurred during the promotional period, with CW Scanner data showing they cost customers $6 on 29 April, before the price went up to $8 on 6 May. The price of a 12-pack of the supermarket’s own-brand fresh cinnamon donuts was increased from $3 to $3.50 on 6 May. It was reduced to $3 again on 18 August. Choice’s senior campaigns and policy adviser, Bea Sherwood, said the advocacy group regularly heard from consumers who said they were confused by the pricing tickets they saw on supermarket shelves. “Prices have changed so much over recent years and we’re seeing them continuously increase, so having an understanding of what a regular shelf price is is not something we can expect consumers to stay on top of,” Sherwood said. “When Woolworths or Coles say something is a standard price, we don’t have the transparency to understand how they’ve come to that.” Explore more on these topics Woolworths Supermarkets Consumer affairs Business news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story RentTech companies asking tenants for personal details ‘completely outside’ new Victorian laws Woolworths posts $1.14bn profit in cost-of-living crisis – but CEO says it’s not thanks to rising shelf prices Woolworths’ Ooshies craze causes Coles sales slump with parents shopping at rival supermarket to collect toys The RBA says rate rises don’t really increase living costs. https://www.politico.eu/article/emmanuel.text: PARIS — President Emmanuel Macron promised that “full transparency will be ensured” as he addressed the nation on Sunday after a weekend of massive unrest across France. Hundreds of thousands of protesters took to the streets nationwide on Saturday, with students joining trade unions and members of the public to protest the cost of living. While the protests were mostly peaceful, footage of mayhem including public buildings being set on fire, stores being looted and clashes with riot police drew widespread condemnation in France and abroad. “Those who destroyed must pay; those who looted must reimburse,” Macron said. Advertisement Advertisement The French government has been accused of mismanaging and underestimating the protests, with calls for Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez to resign emerging both on the left and the far right. According to the latest figures from the French interior ministry, some 2,000 people were arrested during the turmoil. Police, firefighters and demonstrators suffered injuries as the situation unraveled. Serge Papin, France’s minister for small business, will meet with company reps at the Ministry of Economy tomorrow to assess the damage and suggest assistance for businesses that were affected. Macron said he was awaiting “clear answers” on why the protests turned violent. The French president accused “troublemakers from far-left splinter groups, joined by numerous delinquents” of engaging in “unbridled violence.” With six months to go before next year’s presidential election in France, the events of Saturday quickly took on a political dimension. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu also accused the “ultra-left” of fomenting the violence, alleging that the France Unbowed movement and its presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon had played an “important role” within a “far-left network” driving the unrest. Advertisement Advertisement Mélenchon, along with left-wing representatives from several other parties, joined Saturday’s protests and encouraged his supporters to attend, although condemning looting and violence. He said accusations that he was responsible for the mayhem were aimed at weakening his presidential bid, and accused Macron of “letting the situation deteriorate” without offering solutions to appease the anger. Mélenchon is currently in a close race with center-left candidate Raphaël Glucksmann and center-right candidate Edouard Philippe to clinch second place behind far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen in next year’s election. The top two candidates in the election move to a runoff if no candidate wins a majority of votes in the first round. “At stake, too, are France’s image, its credibility, and its influence around the world,” Philippe said ahead of Macron’s statement. “These images of violence have consequences that extend far beyond our borders.” Le Pen and her far-right National Rally have brandished the violent footage to pitch herself as the candidate of an “ appeased France .” The National Rally accused Macron and his government of being the “party of chaos,” and Mélenchon’s France Unbowed of “legitimizing violence.” The protesters had “legitimate social demands,” Le Pen said. “The French people are fed up with being caught between the government’s austerity measures and heavy-handed taxation, and the insurrection activists.” With the U.S. midterms around the corner on Nov. 3, President Donald Trump seized on the violence to blame migration. “France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform Sunday afternoon.
